catalog_quote: It is a principle which can be applied unproblematically to the sample, since the final syllable in most Aslian languages always has the structure /CVC/. The reason for this criterion is that Aslian languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages, seldom have suffixes, and the end of the word is therefore usually part of the root and not affected by synchronic or diachronic morphophonemic processes. Also, the final syllable is the most informative part of a word in that it always receives stress and contains the greatest phonemic variation (Diffloth 1976: 102, p.c.).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation for Aslian (sample explicitly includes Kintaq): word stress falls on the final (major, root) syllable; prefinal minor/presyllables are unstressed or weakly stressed. No Kintaq-specific description of stress was found; the closest first-hand statement is Bishop 1996: 238 for Yala Kensiw ('fixed, non-contrastive primary stress which falls on the final syllable of a lexeme'), a variety Bishop & Peterson regard as the same language as Kintaq.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated for Kintaq. For Kensiw, Bishop 1996: 238 reports secondary stress on the copied initial syllable of reduplicated words; Phaiboon 2006: 208 (Thai NA varieties) describes minor syllables 'with lighter stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Dunn et al. hedge with 'most Aslian languages' for the CVC final-syllable shape, not for stress. Blagden 1906: 773 (generic Semang) claims some di-/polysyllables accent the penult and stress is often 'almost evenly distributed' — pre-modern impression, not confirmed by modern NA descriptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (final syllable of the word = root syllable); statement is typological background in a phylogenetic paper, sourced to Diffloth, not an analysis of Kintaq data. Bishop 1996 (Kensiw) distinguishes citation form (secondary-primary) from casual speech (unstressed-stressed).
new_statements.identity_note: Target is Kintaq [knq], kint1239 (Kintaq Bong / Kentakbong / Kenta' Bong; c. 110 speakers, Bukit Asu (Hulu Perak) and Baling (Kedah), Malaysia; Ethnologue also lists Yala, Thailand). No Kintaq-specific stress statement was found. Bishop & Peterson (quoted in Benjamin 2012: 143) hold that 'Kintaq are linguistically Kensiw' and Dunn et al. 2011 pair Kensiw/Kintaq as near-identical; the first-hand final-stress statement that exists is for Yala Kensiw (Bishop 1996: 238, glottocode kens1248, file../kens1248/). Phaiboon 2006 covers Kansiw (Yala), Tea-de, Yahay (Jahai) and Tean-ean (Ten'edn) but not Kintaq. The quoted Dunn et al. statement is a pan-Aslian generalisation (sourced to Diffloth 1976 on Jah Hut), applied to a sample that includes Kintaq.

sources.note: Family-level: 'the final syllable in most Aslian languages always has the structure /CVC/... the final syllable is the most informative part of a word in that it always receives stress' (p. 300, citing Diffloth 1976: 102). Kintaq (Burenhult 2005 list, Bukit Asu, Hulu Perak; speakers from Lubok Legong, Baling) is one of the sampled varieties (Table 1, p. 299).

sources.citation: Benjamin, Geoffrey. 2012. The Aslian languages of Malaysia and Thailand: an assessment. Language Documentation and Description 11: 136-230. London: SOAS.
sources.note: Sec. 4.2 (p. 179) speaks of the 'major (i.e., stressed, word-final) vowel systems' of Aslian; sec. 4.2.4 (p. 187) quotes Dunn et al. 2011 that the final syllable 'always receives stress'. No Kintaq-specific prosody. p. 143 quotes Bishop & Peterson: ''Kintaq' are linguistically Kensiw, and should therefore not be listed as a separate group'; p. 165 notes Asmah (1964, 1976) as the only Malaysian work on Kintaq.

sources.citation: Phaiboon Duangchan. 2006. Glossary of Aslian languages: the Northern Aslian languages of southern Thailand. Mon-Khmer Studies 36: 207-224.
sources.note: For the four Thai NA varieties Kansiw (Yala), Tea-de, Yahay, Tean-ean (Kintaq NOT included): 'major syllable: a syllable that carries primary stress with a clear vowel sound. Major syllables... only occur in the final syllable of a word'; minor syllable 'with lighter stress'; presyllable reduced (p. 208).

sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 2003. Aslian: Mon-Khmer of the Malay Peninsula. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 1-58.
sources.note: Family survey: sesquisyllabic forms consist of 'a major syllable with fully-stressed vowel, preceded by a minor syllable' (p. 11); examples Senoic; lists Kentaqbong (Kb) among languages but no Kintaq-specific prosody.

sources.citation: Bishop, Nancy M. 1996. A preliminary description of Kensiw (Maniq) phonology. Mon-Khmer Studies 25: 227-253.
sources.note: Sister variety (Yala Kensiw, kens1248), sec. 2.1 p. 238: 'Kensiw has fixed, non-contrastive primary stress which falls on the final syllable of a lexeme'; reduplicated initial syllables bear secondary stress; 'stress is not contrastive in Kensiw'. Relevant because Bishop & Peterson treat Kintaq as linguistically Kensiw, but it is not a description of Kintaq.

sources.note: Evans worked with Kintak Bong but gives no word-accent statement of his own; p. 285 reports Schebesta (1928) that in Jahai 'the accent falls on the last syllable of a word'; pp. 121-122 quote Lloyd on accent in Negrito song metre.

sources.citation: Skeat, Walter W. & Charles O. Blagden. 1906. Pagan Races of the Malay Peninsula, vol. 2 (Part IV Language, by Blagden). London: Macmillan.
sources.note: Grammatical notes, 'Accent', p. 773: 'As a rule, the accent in all the aboriginal dialects appears to fall on the final syllable... In Semang the accent is much weaker than in Sakai... the accent in Semang is usually on the final syllable, yet in some other dissyllables and polysyllables Semang accents the penultimate, and apparently in many cases the stress is almost evenly distributed'. Generic 'Semang' (Northern Aslian), pre-modern.
